# Cementation (blister) steel and case hardening (`cementation_steel`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/materials.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Metallurgy & materials (`materials`)
- Deps: needs bloomery_iron, charcoal_burning; helped by refractories_fireclay, steel_heat_treatment
- Core idea: Carbon soaks slowly into solid red-hot iron. For case hardening, pack finished iron parts in charcoal dust (with horn or leather scraps) in a sealed clay box and keep at orange heat for some hours: the skin becomes steel a millimetre deep and can be quenched hard over a tough core. For bar steel, pack wrought iron bars in charcoal in a sealed stone chest and fire at about 1050–1100 °C for five to seven days; the bars come out blistered and steely throughout, though unevenly, and are bundled, welded and forged to shear steel.
- Pitfalls:
  - Letting air into the chest; the charcoal burns away and the iron scales instead of carburising.
  - Too long or too hot gives cast-iron-like, unforgeable bars.
  - Expecting uniform steel; the outside holds more carbon than the core until it is forged or melted.
  - Phosphoric or slaggy iron gives bad steel; Sheffield depended on pure Swedish bar iron.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1200–1000 BC – carburised iron tools in the Levant and Cyprus; china: c. 5th–6th c. AD – co-fusion steel (wrought iron soaked in molten cast iron), attributed to Qiwu Huaiwen; a different route to the same end; islamic: 9th–11th c. – al-Kindi and al-Biruni classify irons and steels and describe making steel in crucibles; europe: c. 1120 Theophilus case-hardens files; cementation furnaces at Prague (1574) and Nuremberg (1601); 1614 English patent; 1722 Réaumur publishes the process
- Read:
  - René-Antoine Ferchault de Réaumur, L'art de convertir le fer forgé en acier (1722)
  - K. C. Barraclough, Steelmaking Before Bessemer (1984)
